summary: An informational memo that describes in detail the TIFF-F profile of the Tag Image File Format, used for storing facsimile images. It documents the profile that fax software already used.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2306 writes down how a fax page is stored in a TIFF file. Fax software had been doing this for years without anyone agreeing on a definition, so this memo gives the recipe that the existing software follows.

subtitle: The written-down recipe for storing black-and-white fax pages in a TIFF file.

tldr.problem: TIFF-F, the way fax software stored fax pages in TIFF files, had been folklore with no standard reference definition.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC takes Baseline TIFF as a starting point and lists which fields and values a fax file uses, how pages are laid out, and a minimum subset that old readers can handle.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not an Internet standard, and it also defines the faxbw application parameter for the image/tiff media type.

today: RFC 2306 is an Informational memo from March 1998, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents the TIFF-F profile and says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why TIFF-F Needed Writing Down
sections.content:
This document references the Tag Image File Format to define the F profile of TIFF for facsimile, TIFF-F, as a file format for the storage and interchange of facsimile images. The overview says plainly that the TIFF-F encoding had been folklore with no standard reference definition before this document.

The history explains how. Though it had been in common usage for many years, TIFF-F had never been documented in the form of a standard. An informal TIFF-F document was originally created by a small group of fax experts led by Joe Campbell, and the existence of TIFF-F is noted in the TIFF specification but not defined there. Up until TIFF 6.0, TIFF supported various classes that defined its use for particular applications, and in that spirit TIFF-F was known historically as TIFF Class F. As of TIFF 6.0 the class concept was eliminated in favour of Baseline TIFF, so this document updates the definition of TIFF-F as the F profile of TIFF for facsimile, using Baseline TIFF as the starting point and defining the differences that apply to TIFF-F. In almost all cases the resulting fields and values remain consistent with those used historically in earlier definitions of TIFF Class F, and where some values have been updated to give more precise conformance with the ITU-T fax recommendations, the differences are noted.

The memo states its intent in three parts: to document the fields and values applicable to this profile, to define a minimum set of fields and values that should be able to interwork with virtually all historic TIFF-F readers, and to give a broader range of values for the traditional fields that supports the most widely used facsimile compressions, page sizes and resolutions, consistent with the ITU-T T.4 and T.30 recommendations. TIFF-F files are intended for use with the image/tiff MIME media content-type, which includes support for the application parameter, for example application=faxbw.
sections.plainLanguage: Fax software had agreed on a way to store fax pages, but only by word of mouth. This memo writes that agreement down so that different programs can read each other's files.

sections.title: How a TIFF-F File Is Organized
sections.content:
A TIFF file begins with an 8-byte image file header that defines the byte order used within the file, includes a magic number sequence identifying the content as a TIFF file, and then uses an offset to point to the first Image File Directory. An IFD is a sequence of tagged fields, sorted in ascending order by tag value, that holds attributes of an image and pointers to the image data. Each field contains a tag, its type such as short, long or rational, a count indicating the number of values or offsets, and a value or offset. The actual value is present only if it fits into 4 bytes; otherwise an offset points to the data, and that offset may itself point to an array of offsets.

Facsimile documents consist of a series of pages, and in TIFF these may be represented using more than one IFD. Each IFD defines a subfile whose type is given in the NewSubfileType field, and for facsimile data each page of a multi-page document has its own IFD. For bi-level facsimile files the IFDs are organised as a linked list, with the last entry in each IFD pointing to the next, and the pointer in the last IFD is 0. Another technique for organising multiple IFDs as a tree uses the SubIFDs field, but that technique is not applicable to TIFF-F images. Within each IFD the location of the image data is defined by fields associated with strips, which identify the size of strips in rows, the number of bytes per strip after compression, and a strip offset pointing to the actual location of the strip.

The memo then gives five practical guidelines for writing multi-page TIFF-F files, because the structure of TIFF is very flexible and simpler files are easier for readers to process. A writer should present IFDs in the same order as the pages, with pages numbered from 0 upwards, and a reader should expect page order but be able to handle exceptions. The image data for each page should be contained within a single strip, which makes the image easier to find through a single offset and is useful for store and forward messaging where the file is prepared before transmission, though other assumptions may apply for streaming. Each IFD should be placed in the file before the image it describes, with any long field values after their IFD and before the image data. The image data should be placed in a physical order consistent with the logical page order, though readers will need the strip offsets to find the exact physical location either way. Finally, a writer may place the IFD, the value data and the image data before the next image IFD, which the minimum subset files require but which has been relaxed for TIFF-F to reflect past practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The file starts with a small header, then a list of tagged fields describing each page, then the page data itself. Pages are chained together in a list, and the memo suggests writing them in a simple order so that other programs can find them easily.

sections.title: Required Fields and Values
sections.content:
Baseline TIFF requires that the following fields be present for all bi-level images: ImageWidth, ImageLength, Compression, PhotometricInterpretation, StripOffsets, RowsPerStrip, StripByteCounts, XResolution, YResolution and ResolutionUnit. TIFF-F uses all of them but in some cases specifies a different range of acceptable values. If a field is omitted, the Baseline TIFF default applies.

ImageWidth gives the fixed page width in pixels, with the permissible values depending on the X and Y resolutions: 204x98, 204x196, 204x391, 200x100 and 200x200 give widths of 1728, 2048 and 2432; 300x300 gives 2592, 3072 and 3648; and 408x391 and 400x400 give 3456, 4096 and 4864. ImageLength is the total number of scan lines. Compression is 3 or 4, where the Baseline default of 1 for uncompressed data is invalid for facsimile images. PhotometricInterpretation is 0 for normal or 1 for inverted. StripOffsets gives the offset of each strip measured from the beginning of the file, RowsPerStrip the number of scan lines per strip, and StripByteCounts the number of bytes in each strip after compression. ResolutionUnit is 2 for inch or 3 for centimetre, and TIFF-F has traditionally used inch-based measures. XResolution is 204, 200, 300, 400 or 408 per inch, with 200 and 408 added for consistency with T.30, and YResolution is 98, 196, 100, 200, 300, 391 or 400 per inch.

Beyond the Baseline fields, TIFF-F adds required fields. BitsPerSample is 1, because TIFF-F is only used for black-and-white images. FillOrder is 1 or 2; readers must be able to read both bit orders, although the vast majority of facsimile products store data LSB first, exactly as it appears on the telephone line. NewSubFileType is a field of 32 flag bits in which bit 1 is always set to 1 for TIFF-F, indicating a single page of a multi-page image. PageNumber holds two short values, the page number and the total number of pages, so a single-page document uses 0000/0001, and if the second value is 0 the total is not available. SamplesPerPixel is 1. A TIFF-F IFD must also contain either the T4Options or the T6Options field, depending on the setting of the Compression field.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists every value a fax file must contain: how wide the page is, how many lines it has, how it is compressed, and how the bits are stored. Most of them are fixed numbers that a reader can count on.

sections.title: Compression, Page Quality and Optional Fields
sections.content:
The extension fields carry the details of how the page was coded. T4Options is required when Compression is 3. Bit 0 is 0 for one-dimensional data and 1 for two-dimensional Modified READ, bit 1 must be 0 because uncompressed data is not allowed, and bit 2 is 0 for non-byte-aligned EOLs or 1 for byte-aligned EOLs. The field was known as G3Options in earlier versions of TIFF. T6Options is required when Compression is 4; bit 0 set to 0 indicates data compressed with the Modified Modified READ two-dimensional method, which does not use EOLs, and bit 1 must be 0 because uncompressed data does not apply to bi-level facsimile images. This field was known as Group4Options in earlier versions of TIFF. Each MMR encoded image must include an end-of-facsimile-block code at the end of each coded strip.

Three further optional fields describe page quality, and the information is usually obtained from the receiving facsimile hardware. Because Group 3 devices do not necessarily correct errors in the image data, the quality of a received page has to be inferred from the pixel count of decoded scan lines: a good scan line decodes to the correct number of pixels, and a bad one does not. BadFaxLines reports the number of scan lines with an incorrect number of pixels encountered during reception, with PercentBad = (BadFaxLines/ImageLength) * 100. CleanFaxData says whether such lines are still in the data or were regenerated by the receiving device: 0 for data with no bad or regenerated lines, 1 for lines regenerated by the device, and 2 for bad lines left in the data. ConsecutiveBadFaxLines reports the maximum number of consecutive bad lines, which says how the bad lines are distributed and may be a better general indicator of perceived image quality.

The recommended fields are optional and may be ignored by many readers. They are BadFaxLines, CleanFaxData and ConsecutiveBadFaxLines, along with DateTime in the format YYYY:MM:DD HH:MM:SS, with a string length including the NUL byte of 20 bytes, DocumentName, ImageDescription, Orientation and Software. Orientation has a default value of 1, where the 0th row is the visual top of the image and the 0th column the visual left, and an 180-degree rotation is 3; TIFF-F writers should include it even though the default applies if it is omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Two fields say which compression method was used. Three optional fields say how good the received page was, because a fax machine that finds a damaged line often repeats the last good one instead, which looks fine but hides the error.

sections.title: The Minimum Subset and Implementation Warnings
sections.content:
Section 3.6 defines the minimum subset of TIFF-F fields and values that all readers should support to maximise interoperability with current and historical implementations. The minimum requires one bit per sample, Compression 3 for T.4 Modified Huffman, FillOrder 2 for LSB first, an ImageWidth of 1728, NewSubFileType with bit 1 set, PageNumber as page over total with the total in the first IFD, PhotometricInterpretation 0 meaning white, ResolutionUnit 2 for inches, RowsPerStrip equal to ImageLength, SamplesPerPixel 1, T4Options with bit 0 at 0, an XResolution of 204 per inch and a YResolution of 196 or 98 per inch. ImageLength, StripByteCounts and StripOffsets are required but have no fixed minimum value.

For writers of minimum subset files, the file structure is fixed: the IFD of each page precedes the image data for that page, any long field values appear between the IFD and the image data, and each IFD and image pair is immediately followed by the next pair in logical page order. The header's byte order should be II, 0x4949, meaning little-endian, with a version of 42 and an offset of 0x00000008 to the first IFD.

The implementation warnings cover the choices a reader must handle. Uncompressed data is not allowed, so the uncompressed bit in T4Options or T6Options must be 0. Since two-dimensional encoding is not required for Group 3 compatibility, some historic readers cannot read it, which is why the minimum subset requires one-dimensional support, while implementers seeking efficiency should write T.6 MMR files, and readers wanting the most flexibility should support all three of MH, MR and MMR. Almost all facsimile products support both standard 98 dpi and fine 196 dpi vertical resolution, so fine-resolution files are portable, and the higher resolutions added to T.30 in 1993 are supported in the writer even though older terminals and readers may not handle them. T.4 allows certain resolution values to be treated as equivalent, namely 204 and 200, and 400 and 408 horizontally, and 98 and 100, 196 and 200, and 391 and 400 vertically, which permits conversions between inch-based and metric-based terminals.

On end-of-line markers, the historical convention was that all EOLs must be byte-aligned, but Baseline TIFF permits non-byte-aligned EOLs by default and most readers support both, so the minimum subset includes both. Byte alignment means fill bits are added so the first bit of data after an EOL begins on a byte boundary, which spares application software the job of bit-shifting every byte while parsing scan lines. On the Return To Control sequence of 6 consecutive EOLs, writers should not include it, though implementations needing transparency of T.4 image data may include it when the T4Options flags are set for non-byte-aligned data; readers must be able to process files without it and should be able to process files with it. Pages encoded with T.6 MMR must include an end-of-facsimile-block code at the end of each coded strip, followed by pad bits to align on a byte boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: To work with any fax file ever written, a reader needs a minimum set of fields and one standard page layout. The memo gives both, and then lists the odd cases a reader must tolerate, such as files that mark the end of a line in two different ways.

sections.title: MIME Type, Usage and Security
sections.content:
The MIME content-type image/tiff refers to TIFF 6.0 encoded image data. When transported by MIME, the TIFF content defined by this document must be encoded within an image/tiff content type, and an optional application parameter is defined for image/tiff to identify a particular application's subset of TIFF, typically to help the recipient dispatch a suitable rendering package. Because this document defines a facsimile-specific profile of TIFF, the memo defines the parameter value faxbw for black and white facsimile. Applications that use this profile or its minimum subset should set the application parameter to faxbw, giving a content type of image/tiff; application=faxbw. That lets an application recognise the content as being within a profile or subset of TIFF for facsimile before it tries to process the image data.

The usage section says the use of TIFF-F is envisioned as a component of Internet Fax, which may use both a reader and a writer, with the details of the Internet Fax services specified in other documents. It is also a secondary component of the VPIM Message, so that voice messaging systems with fax store-and-forward capability can carry TIFF-F fax messages between compliant systems, and such messages may be rejected if the recipient cannot deal with fax.

The Security Considerations section says the document describes an encoding that creates no security issues beyond those already identified for image/tiff, since the new TIFF fields it defines are purely descriptive and so add no new risks. It also notes that the encoding does not in any way preclude using an Internet security protocol to encrypt, authenticate or non-repudiate TIFF-F encoded facsimile messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Files are sent with the media type image/tiff and an extra parameter, faxbw, that tells the receiver the file holds black-and-white fax pages. The memo adds that fax files can be encrypted or signed like anything else.
